historical_timeline.summary: Works as a compositor in London and feels pain in the bones of his hand over heated type.
Pleurisy that very nearly carried him off.
Severe pleurisy ending in an abscess of the left lung.
Writes the Dialogue between Franklin and the Gout during a gout attack.
Writes to Congress that a long and severe fit of gout the previous winter has shaken him.
First symptoms of the calculous complaint (bladder stone).
Writes that he is subject to the gout and the stone.
Writes that the stone has increased.
Confined chiefly to bed by the stone for his last twelve months, taking laudanum for the worst pain.
Died in Philadelphia after a febrile chest illness.

claims.statement: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston on January 17, 1706 (New Style); an editor's note to his autobiography gives the date as Sunday, January 6, old style, 1706, in a house on Milk Street.

In a letter of July 31, 1786, Franklin recalled that in 1724, as a compositor at Palmer's printing house in London, he sometimes heated his case of type before the fire to warm his hands, until an old workman warned him he might lose the use of his hands, and that he had felt a kind of obscure pain in the bones of his hand when working over very hot type.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own account of occupational exposure to heated type metal, which contains lead.

source_links.locator: Letter on the effects of lead upon the human constitution, Philadelphia, July 31, 1786

claims.statement: A 2008 review of his medical history by Finger and Hagemann concluded that he suffered repeated attacks of gout and a large bladder stone, which caused considerable pain and markedly decreased his mobility.
The same review argues that several factors that raise uric acid converged in him, including sex, genetics, diet, drinking, advanced age, psoriasis, and possible lead poisoning from lead exposure.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective interpretation; lead poisoning is not documented as a diagnosis in his lifetime.

claims.statement: Franklin wrote the Dialogue between Franklin and the Gout, headed Midnight, October 22, 1780, in which the Gout tells him he has eaten and drunk too freely and indulged his indolence; a 2023 rheumatology review states that he woke with a gout attack that night.

In a letter from Passy dated March 12, 1781, to Samuel Huntington, President of Congress, Franklin wrote that he had passed his seventy-fifth year and that the long and severe fit of the gout he had the last winter had shaken him exceedingly, leaving him far from his former bodily strength.

The 1806 edition of his works states that he had been little subject to disease, except an attack of the gout occasionally, until about the year 1781, when he was first attacked with symptoms of the calculous complaint, which continued during his life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Calculous complaint means stone; his later letters identify it as the stone.

claims.statement: In a letter from Passy dated May 23, 1785, to George Wheatley, Franklin agreed that the gout is bad and the stone is worse, and wrote that at fourscore he found himself subject to the gout and the stone.

Writing from Philadelphia on April 15, 1787, he said he had never had the least doubt that his malady was the stone, that it had increased but gave him no more pain than at Passy, and that he thought himself favored to have only the stone and gout; in a letter of October 24, 1788, he wrote that he was recovering from a long-continued gout.
In his autobiography Franklin wrote that at the beginning of February 1726/7 he was taken ill with a pleurisy that very nearly carried him off.

The 1806 edition of his works adds that in 1735 he had a severe pleurisy that ended in an abscess of the left lobe of his lungs, and that a second similar attack some years later left no lasting effect on his breathing.
His autobiography records that he never knew his father or mother to have any sickness but that of which they died, his father Josiah at 89 in 1744 and his mother Abiah at 85 in 1752.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The causes of death are not recorded in the source.

claims.statement: Franklin wrote that in 1736 he lost a son, a boy of four, to smallpox taken in the common way, and regretted that he had not had him inoculated.

His physician's account of his last illness states that the stone had for the last twelve months confined him chiefly to his bed, and that during the most painful paroxysms he took large doses of laudanum.

About sixteen days before his death he developed a fever, then pain in the left side of the chest with cough and labored breathing; an abscess in his lungs burst, and he died in Philadelphia at about eleven at night on April 17, 1790, aged 84.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The contemporary account is reported as written; the modern cause cannot be determined.

claims.statement: A 2023 review describes him as overweight and as probably having had consequences of the metabolic syndrome, including gout.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; no measured weight is used.

assessment.display: Bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia
assessment.assessment: Maximum flow 8.5 mL/s, residual 160 mL, IPSS 16, and a trabeculated bladder with an obstructing median lobe. Obstruction is the probable cause of the stone, and a bladder stone caused by obstruction is an indication for surgery, so both should be treated at one operation
Explained by the stone; cystoscopy shows no tumor, and CT shows no kidney or ureteric lesion. Repeat urinalysis after treatment; further imaging only if hematuria persists
No hydronephrosis; avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxic contrast around surgery

recommendations: Transurethral laser cystolitholapaxy with transurethral resection of the prostate at one operation in about three weeks; send the stone for analysis and the tissue for pathology
Tamsulosin 0.4 mg at bedtime until surgery to ease voiding
No PSA test: at 76 it would not change management, and the resected tissue will be examined
After surgery, repeat urinalysis for red cells and pH, and a 24-hour urine collection for volume, uric acid, citrate, and calcium

If the stone is uric acid: fluids for at least 2.5 L of urine a day, potassium citrate to a urine pH of 6.0 to 6.5 with potassium monitoring because of losartan and kidney disease, and continued allopurinol titration
Check IPSS and post-void residual about one, three, and six months after surgery
